questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following genetic terms:

(i) Epistasis.

(ii) Aneuploidy. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Epistasis** is the **interaction between genes at different loci (non-allelic genes) in which the allele of one gene masks or suppresses the expression of the alleles of another gene**. The gene that masks is **epistatic** and the gene masked is **hypostatic**. Epistasis **modifies the 9:3:3:1 ratio** of a dihybrid cross, e.g. **9:3:4** (recessive epistasis, as in coat colour of mice), **12:3:1** (dominant epistasis), **9:7** (complementary genes) or **15:1** (duplicate genes).

**(ii) Aneuploidy** is a **chromosome mutation in which the cell has one or a few chromosomes more or fewer than the normal diploid number** (so that it is not an exact multiple of the haploid number: $2n \pm 1$), caused by **non-disjunction** of homologous chromosomes or chromatids in meiosis. *Examples:* **trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome, $2n = 47$)**, **Turner's syndrome (XO, $2n = 45$)**, **Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY, $2n = 47$)**. This is different from **polyploidy**, where whole sets of chromosomes are added.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A farmer crossed a cocoa plant that has yellow long pods with another cocoa plant that has red short pods. All the F$_1$ plants produced had yellow long pods. When he crossed the F$_1$ cocoa plants with cocoa plants having red short pods, the following were obtained.

- 483 cocoa plants with yellow long pods.
- 472 cocoa plants with red short pods.
- 103 cocoa plants with yellow short pods.
- 93 plants with red long pods.

(i) Using crosses, explain these results as fully as possible. *[12 marks]*

(ii) Using the figures given, calculate the cross over values between the genes for nature of pod and colour. *[2 marks]*

(iii) Of what importance are linked genes? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Explanation with crosses**

*Symbols.* The F$_1$ are all yellow and long although one parent was red and short, so **yellow (Y) is dominant to red (y)** and **long (L) is dominant to short (l)**; the parents were pure-breeding (homozygous).

**Cross 1 (parents $\rightarrow$ F$_1$)**

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Parental phenotypes | Yellow long $\times$ Red short |
| Parental genotypes | $\dfrac{YL}{YL}$ $\times$ $\dfrac{yl}{yl}$ |
| Gametes | $YL$ and $yl$ |
| F$_1$ genotype | $\dfrac{YL}{yl}$ : all **yellow long** |

**Cross 2 (test cross: F$_1$ $\times$ double recessive)**

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Phenotypes | F$_1$ yellow long $\times$ red short |
| Genotypes | $\dfrac{YL}{yl}$ $\times$ $\dfrac{yl}{yl}$ |
| Gametes of F$_1$ | **Parental types $YL$ and $yl$** (frequent); **recombinant types $Yl$ and $yL$** (rare) |
| Gametes of the red short parent | $yl$ only |

| Offspring genotype | Phenotype | Number | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\dfrac{YL}{yl}$ | Yellow long | 483 | Parental |
| $\dfrac{yl}{yl}$ | Red short | 472 | Parental |
| $\dfrac{Yl}{yl}$ | Yellow short | 103 | Recombinant |
| $\dfrac{yL}{yl}$ | Red long | 93 | Recombinant |

**Interpretation.**

1. If the two genes were on **different chromosomes** (independent assortment), the F$_1$ would make four types of gametes in equal numbers and the test cross would give **1:1:1:1**, i.e. about **288 of each** ($1151 \div 4$). The observed numbers (about **5:5:1:1**) are very different ($\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O-E)^2}{E} \approx 501$ with 3 degrees of freedom, far above the critical value 16.3 at $p = 0.001$), so the genes are **not assorting independently**.
2. The two **parental types are by far the most numerous** (483 + 472 = 955 out of 1151, about 83 %), so the two genes are **linked: they lie on the same chromosome (same linkage group)** and tend to be inherited together. In the F$_1$ the dominant alleles are on one chromosome and the recessive alleles on its homologue (**coupling phase**, $YL/yl$).
3. The linkage is **incomplete**: **recombinant types (103 and 93, about 17 %)** appear because of **crossing over between non-sister chromatids at a chiasma** during **prophase I of meiosis**, which exchanges the alleles and gives the new combinations $Yl$ and $yL$. (With complete linkage only the two parental types would be obtained in the ratio 1:1.)
4. The two recombinant classes are **nearly equal**, as expected since crossing over produces the two reciprocal gametes $Yl$ and $yL$ equally.
5. The cross with the double recessive (red short) parent **reveals the gametes of the F$_1$** directly, because it supplies only $yl$ gametes.

**(ii) Cross-over value**

Total offspring $= 483 + 472 + 103 + 93 = 1151$; recombinants $= 103 + 93 = 196$.

$$\text{Cross-over value} = \frac{\text{number of recombinants}}{\text{total offspring}} \times 100 = \frac{196}{1151} \times 100 = 17.03\ \% \approx 17\ \%$$

The genes for pod colour and pod length are about **17 map units (centimorgans)** apart on the chromosome.

**(iii) Importance of linked genes**

- Genes that are linked are **inherited together**, so **useful combinations of characters are kept** from generation to generation (e.g. high yield with disease resistance in crops and animals), which helps **plant and animal breeders**.
- The crossover values are used to **construct chromosome (genetic) maps** showing the **relative positions of genes**.
- A gene for an inherited disease can be **traced from a linked marker gene**, which allows **prediction of inheritance and genetic screening**.
- Linkage explains the **departures from Mendel's second law** (the ratios obtained in dihybrid crosses), and crossing over still produces **variation** on which natural selection acts.
